title: Resource standards: materials
sub: Lecture 4 + Seminar 4 · standards, target costing, material losses, CMU, Bill of Materials, cutting bars
blurb: Target costing, how much material you really need, the CMU at four levels, and the steel-bar exercise from Test 1.
lede: Test 1 opens with this. The maths is easy; the trouble is mixing up bottles, batches, sheets and metres. Learn the teacher's order of work and the four CMUs he asks for.
six: A **standard** is a reference to compare against. We need standards to **manage** and to **improve**.
**Target costing**: goal price − profit = limit for costs. The question is not how much it costs but how much it **should** cost.
Material requirement = **net (useful) requirement** + technically unavoidable losses (reversible or irreversible).
**CMU** = net useful requirement / total material requirement. Asked at four levels: one cycle, one sheet, the partial sheet, the whole purchase.
Cutting bars: fill the **longest bar** first. When two plans have the same CMU, keep the one with the **bigger leftovers**.
Buy cut-to-size only if the material you lose (**1 − CMU**) is bigger than the supplier's surcharge.
foot: Sources: 3BE216 lecture slides 'Resources Standards' (wine, office chair, metal sheets), Seminar 4, practice Test 1 and its answer key.

questions.answer: A document (reference) with requirements, specifications or guidelines used consistently so things are fit for their purpose
wrong: A certificate you buy from ISO
The fastest time anyone has done the job
A legal contract with a supplier
questions.e: ISO's definition. In operations it is the reference you compare against.

questions.answer: To manage and to improve the operation
wrong: To make the product cheaper for the customer
questions.e: The two words to remember: manage and improve.

questions.q: A cappuccino arrives in 5 seconds instead of the 2-minute standard. What should you think?
questions.answer: Faster is not automatically better: check what went wrong
wrong: Great, lower the standard to 5 seconds
questions.e: From the lecture: finishing much faster than the standard can signal a mistake.

questions.answer: Goal price − profit = the limit for the costs
wrong: Costs are set by the accountant
questions.e: Cost based on price. The state exam asks this.

questions.q: When can you set the price from your costs (cost + profit)?
questions.answer: When you are first in a new market (blue ocean)
questions.e: From the lecture: the first iPhone could. Most firms are in a red ocean where the market already sets the price.

wrong: only what ends up in the product
the material bought in one purchase
questions.e: You must buy more than you use, because some is unavoidably lost.

questions.q: 100 l of wine, 500 ml bottles, losses 0.2 % (pipelines) and 0.3 % (bottling). How many bottles can you promise?
questions.e: Each bottle needs 500 + 1 + 1.5 = 502.5 ml; 100 000 / 502.5 = 199.0… A half bottle is not a product.

questions.answer: net useful requirement / total material requirement
wrong: the price of the material per kg
questions.e: Coefficient of Material Utilization: how much of what you buy you really use.

questions.answer: a document listing the parts of each product and how many of each
questions.e: The product structure plus the quantity of each part.

questions.q: 100 chairs × 5 arms; one 1 m² sheet gives 18 arms; sheets come in packs of 5. How many sheets do you buy?
Why is the CMU of one press cycle the same (78.54 %) for the normal and the kids' chair?
questions.answer: The geometry is the same: two ellipses in a square
wrong: Because the kids' chair is 20 % smaller
questions.e: Same shape, same proportions, same CMU.

questions.q: Why is the kids' chair better per sheet (72.38 % vs 63.62 %)?
questions.answer: More ellipses fit, and the leftover strip is smaller
questions.e: 24 × 24 squares: 4 per side, a small strip left; 30 × 30: 3 per side, a 10 cm strip left.

questions.q: Why is the kids' chair WORSE for the whole purchase (≈56.5 % vs 58.9 %)?
questions.answer: Four bought sheets stay unused (CMU 0) instead of two
questions.e: 16 sheets needed, 20 bought: 4 at 0 %. The normal chair: 28 needed, 30 bought: 2 at 0 %.

questions.q: By analogy the kids' chair (20 % smaller) needs 25 sheets; by calculation it needs…
questions.e: 32 arms per sheet → 500 / 32 = 15.6 → 16 sheets → buy 20. Analogy is quick but can be far off.

questions.q: Two bar plans have the same CMU. Which one does the teacher want?
questions.answer: The one with the bigger leftover pieces
wrong: The one with more 6 m bars
The one with the smaller leftover pieces
questions.e: Big leftovers are easier to sell or reuse. Small offcuts lose the points.

questions.q: CMU 96.11 %. The supplier cuts to size for 5 % extra. Take it?
questions.answer: No: you lose only 3.89 %, less than 5 %
wrong: Yes: cut pieces are always better

questions.q: Can you sell the material burnt away by the saw?
questions.answer: No: it doesn't exist any more
questions.e: In Test 1 the leftover to sell is 3.38 m, not 3.5 m, because the cuts burn material.

questions.q: How can the CMU of the whole purchase be improved?
questions.answer: Reuse unused sheets from stock across orders during the year
questions.e: Per order the number doesn't change; across a year, leftover sheets in the warehouse can be used by the next order. Redesigning the shape is what improves the cycle CMU.

vocab.meaning: A reference document with requirements or specifications, used to manage and improve.
Standards for material, labour and other resources.
Cost based on price: goal price − profit = the limit for costs.
A new market where you are first and set the price yourself.
An existing market where the price is already set.
Calculate the material piece by piece.
Estimate from a similar product (20 % smaller → 20 % less material).
The material that ends up in the product.
Material you must buy but will lose (pipelines, cutting, spills).
A loss you can bring back (spilled rice back on the plate).
A loss you can't get back (burnt, thrown away).
Coefficient of Material Utilization: net useful requirement / total material requirement.
The list of parts of a product and how many of each.
The material the saw cuts away; it can't be sold.

facts: We need standards to manage and to {improve|certify|sell|hire}.
In target costing the goal price minus the profit gives the limit for {costs|sales|wages|taxes}.
Material lost in the pipelines is a technically {unavoidable|optional|reversible|useful} loss.
From 100 l of wine you can promise {199|200|198|201} bottles of 500 ml.
The CMU of the wine barrel is {99.5|100|99|95} %.
One 30 × 30 cm square gives a CMU of {78.54|63.62|49.48|58.90} %.
If a sheet is not used at all in the order, its CMU is {0|50|100|25} %.
If two bar plans have the same CMU, keep the one with the {bigger|smaller|fewer|cheaper} leftovers.
sheet: CMU 90.10 % → lose 9.9 % now vs 13.89 % waiting → go now
